title: It Wisnae Us: The Truth About Glasgow and Slavery
author: Stephen Mullen
place: Gallery of Modern Art, Royal Exchange Square
description: Historian Stephen Mullen’s short guide to how Atlantic slavery paid for the city centre. Tobacco lord William Cunninghame built a mansion in 1778 off Queen Street. It is now the Gallery of Modern Art. The title is Scots for “it wasn’t us.”

title: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
author: Alan Crawford
place: Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh Building
description: Architectural historian Alan Crawford’s compact illustrated life of Glasgow’s great architect and designer. His masterpiece was the Glasgow School of Art building on Renfrew Street. It burned in 2014 and again in 2018. Restoration is still under way.

title: Tea and Taste: The Glasgow Tea Rooms 1875–1975
author: Perilla Kinchin
place: Willow Tea Rooms building, Sauchiehall Street
description: Design historian Perilla Kinchin on how Glasgow, a city of temperance campaigners, built a tea-room culture. Businesswoman Kate Cranston hired Mackintosh to design the Willow Tea Rooms on Sauchiehall Street in 1903. You can still have tea there.

title: When the Clyde Ran Red: A Social History of Red Clydeside
author: Maggie Craig
description: Historian Maggie Craig on Red Clydeside, the strikes and protests of 1910–1922. In 1915 Govan housewife Mary Barbour led a rent strike that forced a national rent freeze. Her statue has stood at Govan Cross, the old town square, since 2018.

title: Growing Up in the Gorbals
author: Ralph Glasser
description: Ralph Glasser’s memoir of a poor Jewish childhood in the Gorbals tenements, south of the river, in the 1920s and ’30s. He worked in a barber’s and a garment factory, won a place at Oxford, and cycled there. The tenements were cleared in the 1960s.

title: Lanark
author: Alasdair Gray
description: Novelist and painter Alasdair Gray’s novel, half realist, half fantasy. Its hero, art student Duncan Thaw, grows up in Riddrie, the east-end council estate where Gray grew up. It argues that Glasgow needs artists to imagine it. It’s long.

title: Windswept & Interesting
author: Billy Connolly
place: Site of Alexander Stephen & Sons shipyard, Linthouse
description: Comedian Billy Connolly’s memoir of a hard Glasgow boyhood and how he found his voice. Before folk music and stand-up he was a welder at Alexander Stephen & Sons, a shipyard at Linthouse on the Clyde. The yard closed in 1968. It is very funny.

title: New Selected Poems
author: Edwin Morgan
description: Poems by Edwin Morgan, Glasgow’s first poet laureate and later Scotland’s national poet. He wrote about the city for sixty years: tenements, demolitions, a Glasgow Green park poem about men meeting in the dark. He came out publicly at seventy.

title: Jock Stein: The Definitive Biography
author: Archie Macpherson
description: Broadcaster Archie Macpherson’s life of the former miner who managed Celtic Football Club. In 1967 his team, all born near Glasgow, became the first British side to win the European Cup. Their ground is Celtic Park, the stadium in Parkhead.

title: Laidlaw
author: William McIlvanney
description: Novelist William McIlvanney’s first Glasgow detective story, often called the start of Scottish crime writing known as Tartan Noir. A girl is found murdered in Kelvingrove Park, the Victorian park in the West End. The city’s pubs and streets do the rest.

title: Shuggie Bain
author: Douglas Stuart
description: Douglas Stuart’s Booker Prize-winning novel about a boy and his alcoholic mother in 1980s Glasgow, as the shipyards and pits closed. It begins in the Sighthill tower blocks north of the centre. The towers were demolished in 2016. Stuart grew up there.
